You say that you have someone do something, let someone do something, or that something happens to you, with faire, laisser, se faire, se laisser and se voir + infinitive.
Don’t let yourself be pushed around.
The mayor was refused the budget.
Use faire + infinitive to say you have someone else do an action.
Place pronouns correctly before “faire” and know that “fait” stays invariable.
Use se faire + infinitive for what happens to you (se faire voler) or what you have done for you (se faire couper les cheveux).
Use laisser and se laisser + infinitive.
Recognise and use the formal passive se voir + infinitive.
Tuesday, 20 April 2032. On the Grenoble site, a former glove factory that will become a music hall, Radu is waiting for Julien in front of a pile of planks. Lucia is due to give birth in two weeks.
Look at this wood. I got conned. The supplier sold me wet fir at the price of oak.
Can’t you make him take it back?
I tried. He refuses. He says I let him deliver without checking, so it’s my fault.
Don’t let him push you around. Have the wood checked by an expert, and send him the report by registered mail.
That’s what I’m going to do. But in the meantime, the site is falling behind. And I have to bring the carpenters over from Lyon.
And the town hall? The mayor had promised you he would fund the roof.
The mayor was refused the budget by his town council. He can’t do anything before June.
Then we’ll get help some other way. Amina knows a foundation that funds this kind of project.
You know what Lucia told me this morning? “If you leave me alone the week of the birth, I’ll make you sleep on the building site.”
(he laughs) She’s right. Let me take care of Grenoble. You go back to Lyon.
You? You can’t even tell the difference between a beam and a post.
Exactly. I’ll have everything explained to me. And I’ll have you check everything, on the phone, every evening.
to do; to have someone do
“Zhum swee fay”: the “e” of “me” drops in fast speech.
“Faire + infinitive” shows that you do NOT do the action yourself, but have someone else do it. Romanian uses “a pune pe cineva să”, “a da la” or simply “a(-și) face”:
She is having a house built.
The carpenters must be brought over.
Watch out for “faire faire”: “Je fais faire les plans.” = I have someone draw up the plans. It is perfectly correct!
The object pronoun goes before “faire”, not before the infinitive. If the person doing the action is also mentioned, they become “à” (lui/leur) or “par”:
Je fais lire la lettre à Julien.
Fais vérifier le bois par un expert.
The participle “fait” followed by an infinitive stays INVARIABLE: “Je les ai fait venir” (not “faits”), “Elle s’est fait couper les cheveux” (not “faite”).
“Se faire + infinitive” has two meanings. The context shows which:
Il s’est fait voler son portefeuille.
you have it done for you
Very common expressions: se faire avoir / rouler (to be conned), se faire engueuler (to get told off, informal), se faire comprendre (to make yourself understood).
“Laisser + infinitive” = to allow, not to prevent. “Se laisser + infinitive” = to let yourself be (convinced, fooled, carried):
I let him deliver without checking.
Don’t let yourself be pushed around! (react)
Unlike “fait”, the participle “laissé” followed by an infinitive may or may not agree: “Je les ai laissé(s) partir.” Modern spelling (1990) recommends the invariable form.
5. Se voir + infinitive: the formal passive

In formal register (press, administration), “se voir + infinitive” replaces a passive that is impossible in French. Verbs like “refuser, confier, offrir, accorder” take an indirect object, so they cannot have an ordinary passive:
Radu was entrusted with managing the works.
She was offered a job in Paris.
“Le maire a été refusé le budget” ✗ is impossible in French. Use “se voir refuser” or the active: “Le conseil a refusé le budget au maire.”
“I had the workers come.” (with a pronoun)
Le maire a été refusé le budget.
Le maire s’est vu refuser le budget.
Le maire s’est fait refusé le budget.
Don’t let yourself be pushed around!
Quel bois le fournisseur a-t-il vendu à Radu ?
Pourquoi le maire ne peut-il pas financer le toit ?
Il s’est vu refuser le budget
De faire vérifier le bois par un expert
I have to bring the carpenters over from Lyon.
I’m having an expert check the wood.

On Tuesday 13 April, at ten past eight, Inès was on the radio. It was a big morning programme that millions of people listened to while drinking their coffee or driving. The journalist had brought her to Paris the day before, with her mother, and had booked them a hotel room near the studio. Inès had hardly slept. She had spent the night looking at the city lights through the window.

The journalist first had her talk about the contest, the Odéon, the silence. Then he asked her what she had done since. Inès hesitated. She looked at her mother, behind the studio glass. Her mother nodded. So Inès told the story of the sea. Farid’s boat, the Dakar cassette, the ashes, the lime flowers floating, yellow on blue. She spoke for four minutes without the journalist interrupting her once.

When she stopped, there were three seconds of silence on air. On the radio, three seconds is an eternity. Then the journalist cleared his throat and said, in a slightly changed voice: “Well… I think we’ll let a little music play.” And he played Henri’s waltz, recorded by the La Duchère orchestra, with the eight bars of silence.

The radio switchboard exploded. All morning, listeners called to tell their own story of silence. A lorry driver who whistled for his mother. A nurse from Brest. An old gentleman who had lost his wife and always left an empty place at the table. And among all those calls, there was one nobody expected.

It came from Mirecourt, a small town in the Vosges, famous for three centuries for its violin makers. The man’s name was Gérard Thiébaut. He was seventy-nine and a retired luthier. He wanted to know whether the network’s orchestras had damaged instruments. If so, he offered to have them sent to him and repair them himself, free of charge, until the end of his days.

Amina received the information at a quarter past nine. By ten, she had opened a spreadsheet titled “Damaged instruments”. By noon, all twelve orchestras had replied. There were forty-three instruments to repair: cracked violins, broken bows, a double bass that had been hit by a football in Toulouse, and three clarinets whose keys no longer closed.

Gérard Thiébaut was not put off by the number. “Forty-three?” he said on the phone. “Very good. That will give me two years of work. At my age, it’s an excellent reason to stay alive.” The first lorry left Lyon at the end of April. Yanis’s red cello, which had had a crack since the winter, was in the first crate.

Yanis didn’t want to let it go. He was twelve now, and had played that cello for four years. He asked whether he could go with it to Mirecourt. Théo explained that it wasn’t possible. So Yanis slipped a little note for the luthier into the case: “Sir, take care of him. He has a difficult character, but he sings well.”

Meanwhile, Julien and Radu had started the big project of the year. The ministry had confirmed the eight new cities for 2033. So eight halls had to be built or renovated in less than a year. Radu had been entrusted with the technical management of all the works. It was the biggest project of his life. It was also the worst possible moment, since his wife was due to give birth in May.

The first site was in Grenoble. The city had offered a former glove factory at the foot of the mountains, abandoned for twenty years. Radu had loved it at once. The brick walls were solid, the windows huge, and through the broken roof you could see the peaks still covered in snow. “We’ll let the light in through there,” he had said, pointing at the hole. “Like at La Duchère.”

But on 20 April, when Julien came to visit the site, Radu was waiting for him in front of a pile of planks with a face like a funeral. The timber supplier had delivered wet fir, full of knots, at the price of oak. Radu had let him unload without checking, because he was on the phone with Lucia. He had been conned like a beginner, and he couldn’t forgive himself.

Julien listened without interrupting. Then he advised him not to let himself be pushed around, to have the wood examined by an expert and to send a registered letter to the supplier. Radu wrote the letter that very evening, in his hotel room, having Lucia correct every sentence over the phone. Lucia corrected very well. She also corrected a lot.

There was another problem. The mayor of Grenoble, who had promised to fund the roof, had been refused the budget by his town council. He couldn’t do anything before June. Now, no roof means no hall, and no hall means no orchestra. Julien called Amina. Amina called a foundation. The foundation asked for a file. Amina sent it that same evening. She had already prepared it, just in case.

The next day, Julien made a decision. He had Radu sit down on a crate in the middle of the empty factory and told him he was going back to Lyon. Right away. Julien would stay in Grenoble to supervise the site. Radu protested. Julien couldn’t even tell a beam from a post. “Exactly,” Julien replied. “I’ll have everything explained to me. By you. On the phone. Every evening.”

Radu let himself be convinced. It must be said that Lucia had warned him that very morning, on the phone, in a very calm voice: “If you leave me alone the week of the birth, I’ll make you sleep on the building site until the end of the year.” Radu knew his wife. When Lucia spoke very calmly, it was better to do what she said.

So Julien stayed in Grenoble for ten days. He learnt more about carpentry than he had in forty years. He learnt that oak isn’t worked like fir, that a beam carries and a post supports, and that you never trust a supplier who smiles too much. Every evening, Radu had him recite his lesson on the phone, like a schoolboy.

The expert came on 26 April. He stuck a little machine into the planks, looked at the figures and pulled a face. “Thirty-two percent moisture,” he said. “This wood should have dried for another two years. You’ve been ripped off, sir.” Julien sent a photo of the report to Radu. Radu sent a photo of the report to the supplier. The supplier called back within the hour.

The wood was taken back the next day and replaced with dry oak at no extra charge. The supplier even made a point of coming to apologise in person, with a bottle of green Chartreuse. Julien kept it for Radu. And on 28 April, the foundation called Amina: it agreed to fund the Grenoble roof. Amina hung up, opened a new spreadsheet, then called Julien.

In Lyon, meanwhile, Elena had arrived from Iași on 25 April, with two suitcases and a list. This time Grandma hadn’t made the trip. She was eighty-six, and the doctor had forbidden her the coach. She had protested for a week, then let herself be persuaded, on condition that she be shown the baby by video within an hour of the birth.

Elena’s list ran to three pages. It was mostly about the baby’s room, which Radu hadn’t finished, and the soup Lucia would have to be made to eat after the birth. Radu, back from Grenoble, spent three days painting, assembling furniture and putting up shelves under his mother’s supervision. Elena wouldn’t let him do anything alone. She said she knew him.

Rose-Hélène, for her part, was preparing the baby in her own way. She had been four since March, and now considered herself an expert on little brothers. She had made a list of what the baby would have to learn: to walk, to whistle, not to touch the harmonica, and to leave Henri-Ion alone. Henri-Ion, who now walked everywhere, didn’t seem convinced by the last point.

On Monday 3 May, the city of Lyon planted a lime tree in the Parc de la Tête d’Or. It was the result of Bernard Delorme’s motion. The council had wanted a tree “for Odile, and for all those who whistle”, and Isabelle had chosen the spot and the date. 3 May, because it was the date written under the lime flower Henri had picked in that same park in 1962.

There were a lot of people. The sixty La Duchère children in blue T-shirts. Mrs Roux in a wheelchair, pushed by Inès. Claire Vasseur, Amina, Théo, Isabelle. Yves Le Goff, who had arrived from Nantes the day before with his cast-iron pan and announced that he wouldn’t leave before seeing the baby. And Lucia, enormous, a few days from her due date, who had refused to stay at home.

Bernard Delorme gave a very short speech. He said that for years he had been the man who said no. No to the hall, no to the orchestra, no to useless spending. “I let myself be changed,” he said. “By an old lady I never met, and by a teenager who beat me at the game I thought I knew best: arguments.”

Then Rose-Hélène was brought forward. She was to put in the first spadeful of earth, with a little red spade the park gardener had lent her. She took her job very seriously. She put in the earth, pressed it down with her feet, watered it with a watering can almost as big as herself, then took the harmonica out of her pocket.

The sixty children played the waltz. At the moment of silence, under the young lime tree, among the Monday strollers who had stopped without understanding, Rose-Hélène whistled. And this time Henri-Ion, in his father’s arms, blew along with her. Still without a note. But with great conviction. Yves Le Goff took out his handkerchief. He was beginning to get used to it.

It was at that moment that Lucia took Radu’s arm and said, very calmly: “Radu. I think someone should drive me to the hospital.” Radu looked at her without understanding. Then he understood. He dropped the ceremony programme, shouted “Now?”, and sixty children turned round at the same moment.

What followed, Isabelle later told like a scene from a comedy. Radu ran in every direction without knowing where he had parked the car. Elena shouted instructions in Romanian. Mrs Roux, from her wheelchair, gave midwife’s advice dating from 1965. Only Lucia stayed perfectly calm, sitting on a bench, breathing as she had been taught.

In the end, it was Théo who took charge. He sat Lucia in his own car, parked right in front of the park gates. He had Radu get in beside her and Elena in the back. Then he drove to the Croix-Rousse hospital without once exceeding the speed limit, which Radu reproached him for the whole way.

Ioana and Julien went back to rue d’Austerlitz with the children. Yves came with them. He had offered to look after them overnight, so that Ioana could go to the hospital if she was needed. Julien hesitated. Yves was eighty-eight, with a cane and no experience of four-year-olds. But Rose-Hélène settled it: she wanted galettes for dinner.

Yves made the galettes. He had Rose-Hélène set the table. He had Henri-Ion taste salted butter; the boy pulled a terrible face and asked for more. After dinner he told them stories of storms, whales and faraway ports, until the two children fell asleep on the sofa, one against the other. Then he sat down in the armchair and waited.

At the hospital, the night was long. Radu couldn’t keep still. He walked up and down the corridor, sat down, stood up, asked every passing nurse for news. Around two in the morning, a midwife let him into the delivery room, warning him that if he fainted, they would leave him on the floor. He didn’t faint. Almost not.

The baby was born on Tuesday 4 May 2032, at twelve minutes past six, at the very moment the sun was rising over the Croix-Rousse hill. It was a boy of three kilos four hundred, with lots of black hair and a very powerful voice. It was also Radu and Lucia’s second wedding anniversary. Radu, in tears, said it was the most beautiful anniversary present in history.

Elena called Iași at twenty past six. It was twenty past seven in Romania. Grandma had been waiting by her phone since five in the morning, dressed, hair done, wearing her Sunday headscarf. When she saw the baby on the screen, she said nothing for a long moment. Then she asked what his name was.

Lucia smiled. She had kept the secret for three months. She hadn’t told anyone, not even Radu, who had tried every possible way to make her confess. She looked at the screen, then at Radu, then at the baby. “His name is Yves,” she said. “Like the sailor.” Grandma nodded, as if it were obvious. Then she said she had dreamt of a boat.

It took Radu several seconds to understand. Then he burst out laughing. “Yves! You got me! You let me talk about Romanian names for three months!” Lucia replied that he had set the conditions himself: a name that can be pronounced in Romanian and in French, and that isn’t already taken in the family. “Yves,” she said, “isn’t family yet. Well, not officially.”

At the same moment, on rue d’Austerlitz, Ioana’s phone rang. Ioana listened, smiled, then passed the phone to Yves, who hadn’t gone to bed all night. It was Lucia. She wanted to tell him herself. Yves listened without a word. Then he put the phone down on his knees, very slowly, and stayed motionless, his eyes fixed on the window.

Rose-Hélène woke up and found him like that. She asked him if he was sad. He shook his head. Then she asked him why he was crying. Yves took a long time to answer. “Because in eighty-eight years,” he finally said, “nobody had ever given me anything so big. Not even the sea.”

He went to the hospital at ten, with Julien and the two children. He had put on a tie. Nobody had ever seen him in a tie. In the room, Lucia motioned him to sit in the armchair by the window. Then the nurse put the baby in his arms. Yves held little Yves the way you hold a precious sea chart, with both hands, without moving.

“I’d like to ask you something,” said Lucia. “Radu and I would like you to be his godfather.” Yves looked up. He said he was far too old, that he wouldn’t see him grow up, that they should choose someone younger. Lucia shook her head. “That’s exactly why,” she replied. “He needs someone to teach him the important things straight away.”

Yves thought for a long moment. Then he accepted, on his own terms. He would teach the little one to tie sailor’s knots, to recognise the stars, and to make buckwheat galettes. He would have him listen to the Dakar cassette as soon as he was old enough to understand what a friend is. And he would never let him get on a boat without a life jacket. Radu said that seemed reasonable.

Meanwhile, Rose-Hélène was examining her cousin with a very critical eye. She declared that he was small, red and noisy, and that he looked like Henri-Ion as a baby, which was not a compliment. Henri-Ion, for his part, was eyeing the newcomer suspiciously. He had just realised he was no longer the youngest in the family, and he didn’t like the news at all.

Around noon, little Yves started to cry. Not a little whimper: a real sailor’s cry, powerful, furious, making the windows shake. Lucia rocked him. Radu walked him around. The nurse checked he didn’t need anything. Nothing worked. Then Rose-Hélène went up to the cot, took out Henri’s harmonica, and played the three notes, very softly.

The baby fell silent at once. He opened his eyes, big dark eyes that could still see almost nothing, and turned his head towards the sound. Rose-Hélène whistled the next three notes. The baby didn’t move. She carried on, the whole waltz, half played, half whistled, with her usual wrong notes. When she stopped, little Yves was asleep.

In the room, nobody dared speak. The nurse, in the doorway, asked in a whisper who had taught the little girl that. Julien answered: “A neighbour.” The nurse asked whether the neighbour could come and teach the same thing to her son, who never slept. Julien smiled. He said the neighbour was no longer here, but that his daughter gave lessons. Free. On Tuesdays.

In the afternoon, Inès came to the maternity ward with Théo. She had brought a present she had had made by an engraver in the Croix-Rousse: a little wooden plaque engraved with the eight bars of silence of the waltz, without a single note, only rests. “For his room,” she told Lucia. “That way he’ll know from the start that you have to leave room for others.” Lucia hugged her without saying anything.

The same day, a parcel arrived at La Duchère from Mirecourt. Gérard Thiébaut had repaired Yanis’s red cello as a priority. In the case, next to Yanis’s little note, he had slipped his reply: “Young man, your cello does indeed have a difficult character. I let it express itself. It sings better than before. Take care of it.” Yanis played all evening without stopping.

In the evening, Julien had to go back to Grenoble. The carpenters were arriving the next morning and he had promised to be there to get them started. On the train, he called Radu for the evening lesson. But Radu didn’t want to talk about beams. He wanted to talk about his son. For an hour he described his hands, his feet, his hair, the way he frowned.

Julien let him talk. He remembered Rose-Hélène’s birth, and Henri-Ion’s, that feeling of suddenly holding the whole world in your hands. At the end, Radu fell silent. Then he said: “You know, Julien, I think I finally understand why we build halls. It’s not for the walls. It’s for the people who will come after us.”

The next day, in Grenoble, the sun was shining on the mountains. The carpenters arrived at seven, with the dry oak and Radu’s plans. Julien let them into the empty factory. The foreman, a tall bearded man named Joseph, looked at the broken roof, the brick walls, the snowy peaks. Then he asked what was going to happen in this hall.

Julien explained. The children, the instruments, the orchestra, the waltz. He talked about Odile, about the window in the roof, about the eight bars of silence. Joseph listened, stroking his beard. Then he said he had a nine-year-old grandson who did nothing at school and drummed on every table with pencils. He asked whether they would take a drummer.

Julien said yes, of course, and that they should in fact let him try the timpani. Joseph nodded, satisfied. Then he turned to his men and shouted: “Come on, lads! We’ve got a roof to build, and the light has to get through!” And under the Alpine sky, the first hammer blows rang out in the old glove factory.

That night, Yves Le Goff slept in Odile’s flat for the first time. Isabelle had insisted. There was a spare room, and she didn’t want her nephew-by-heart’s godfather sleeping in a hotel. Yves lay down in the little bed in the guest room, under an old photo of the Vieux-Port. It took him a long time to fall asleep.

Around midnight, he got up. He went into the living room, sat down in Odile’s armchair by the window, and looked at the lights of Fourvière. Then, very softly, so as not to wake anyone, he whistled the first three notes of the waltz. Off-key, as always. He had always whistled off-key. Henri already reproached him for it in 1978.

And on the other side of the landing, through two doors and a wall, a small sleepy voice answered with the next three notes. Rose-Hélène. She hadn’t even woken up. Yves smiled in the dark. He thought of Henri, of Odile, of little Yves sleeping at the Croix-Rousse. He thought that the waltz now had a new sailor on board. Then he went back to bed and fell asleep at once.

The registered letter Radu sends to the timber supplier, corrected by Lucia on the phone. It is a model DELF B2 formal letter. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Dear Sir, on 15 April, your company delivered twenty cubic metres of timber to our Grenoble site, ordered under number 2032-118. I am writing to you because this delivery does not match our order.

Indeed, we had ordered dry oak. Now, you had wet fir delivered to us, full of knots, at the price of oak. I admit that I let your employees unload the wood without checking it. However, that does not change your mistake in any way.

I had the wood examined by an independent expert, who measured a moisture level of thirty-two percent. Please find his report attached. This wood cannot under any circumstances be used for a roof frame.
Consequently, I ask you to have this wood collected as soon as possible and replaced with dry oak, in accordance with our order, at no extra charge.
I have no doubt that you will understand the situation. However, I must point out that if I receive no reply from you within eight days, I shall be obliged to consult a lawyer.
I look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully, — Radu Popescu, technical director, “Musique en partage” network
